# DeliveryIQ: findings summary

*Generated by `scripts/generate_findings.py` on 2026-10-23 from `data/processed/orders_delivered.parquet`,
`data/processed/data_quality_report.json` and `models/model_metrics.json`. Do not edit by hand: every number below is computed by the script.
Regenerate with `.venv/bin/python scripts/generate_findings.py`.*

## Read this first

* This is a **descriptive** analysis of historical Olist orders (2016-2018). Every finding is an **association**. Nothing here shows what *causes* a late delivery.
* Segment screens (state, category, route) test many segments at once at the 95% level **without adjusting for multiple comparisons** (the month screen is Bonferroni-adjusted).
  A flagged segment is a **lead to investigate**, not a confirmed effect, and several flags would be expected by chance alone.
* Late rates were **not stable over time** (section 4), and some relationships changed sign or weakened between time windows (sections 5 to 9). Figures averaged over the whole history can mislead about any one period.
* The prediction model's out-of-sample (later-window) performance is **modest**; see section 9 for the numbers before relying on any score.
* "Late" = delivered on a calendar date after the estimated delivery date. "Orders" means delivered orders with valid dates unless stated.

## 1. Dataset scope

Source: the public Olist Brazilian e-commerce dataset (Kaggle), as read by `src/preprocessing.py`. All numbers below
describe **delivered orders with valid dates** unless stated otherwise.

* Orders in the raw file: **99,441** (one row per order; 112,650 item rows, 3,095 sellers).
* Purchase-date range of all orders: 2016-09-04 to 2018-10-17.
* **Analysis set (delivered, all three dates present, delivery not before purchase): 96,470 orders**
  (97.0% of all orders). Purchase-date range of the analysis set: 2016-09-15 to 2018-08-29.
* Excluded: 2,963 orders with a non-delivered status and 8 delivered orders with no delivery date.
  They have no outcome and are never counted as on time.
* "Late" means the calendar date of customer delivery is after the calendar date of the estimated delivery
  (calendar date of customer delivery > calendar date of estimated delivery). Under a stricter timestamp-based definition the late rate would be 8.11% instead of 6.77%.
* Customers are in 27 states, sellers in 22 states, products fall into 74 categories.
* Months with fewer than 100 analysed orders (too sparse to interpret): 2016-09 (n=1), 2016-12 (n=1).

Order status in the raw file:

## 2. Overall late rate

* **6.77% of delivered orders arrived after the estimated date** (6,534 of 96,470; 95% Wilson interval 6.6% to 6.9%).
* 91.9% arrived before the estimated date, 1.3% on the estimated date.
* Late orders were late by a mean of 10.6 days (median 7.0, 90th percentile 22.0, maximum 188).

This is the average over the whole 2016-2018 history. Section 4 shows that the rate moved a lot between periods, so the
overall figure is not a stable property of the marketplace.

## 3. Delivery-time distribution

Delivery time = purchase to customer delivery, in days (n = 96,470).

| Statistic | Days |

| mean | 12.6 |
| median | 10.2 |
| standard deviation | 9.5 |
| 90th percentile | 23.1 |
| 95th percentile | 29.3 |
| minimum | 0.5 |
| maximum | 209.6 |
| skewness | 3.83 |

The distribution is right-skewed (skewness 3.83; mean 12.6 days is above the median 10.2). Share delivered within 14 days: 68.7%; within 30 days: 95.3%; more than 30 days: 4.7%.

| Delivery time | Orders | Share |
| :-- | --: | --: |
| up to 7 days | 26,046 | 27.0% |
| 7-14 days | 40,212 | 41.7% |
| 14-21 days | 17,713 | 18.4% |
| 21-30 days | 7,949 | 8.2% |
| more than 30 days | 4,550 | 4.7% |

The delivery promise shown at checkout (estimated date minus purchase date) has a median of 24.0 days
(mean 24.4, 10th to 90th percentile 14 to 35 days). Promises are typically longer than actual delivery times (median promise 24.0 vs median delivery 10.2 days), which is why most orders arrive early or on the estimated date.

Months compared with the pooled remaining months (two-proportion test, Bonferroni-adjusted over 21 months with n >= 100).
3 months stand out as markedly higher:

* 2018-03: 19.0% late (n = 7,003) vs 5.8% in all other months; difference +13.1 pp (95% CI +12.2 pp to +14.1 pp)
* 2018-02: 14.1% late (n = 6,555) vs 6.2% in all other months; difference +7.9 pp (95% CI +7.1 pp to +8.8 pp)
* 2017-11: 12.4% late (n = 7,288) vs 6.3% in all other months; difference +6.1 pp (95% CI +5.3 pp to +6.9 pp)

The median monthly late rate (months with n >= 100) is 4.4%, so these months are several times the typical level.
The rate is **not stationary** (highest month 19.0%, lowest reliable month 0.8%).
This table cannot say why. Possible explanations (for example seasonal demand peaks or carrier disruption) are hypotheses; nothing in this data tests them.

**The cross-state minus same-state gap changes sign between windows (+5.1 pp, +3.1 pp, -4.4 pp in the windows in the order shown).** Over the full history cross-state orders are later, but in the most recent window the relationship is reversed. A route or same-state pattern learned from the earlier data therefore need not hold for later orders; this matters directly for the prediction model (section 9).

Mean delivery time over the full history: cross-state 15.1 days vs same-state 7.9 days.

## 8. Other associations

* Customer state vs late delivery: chi-square = 1,782.4, df = 25, Cramer's V = 0.136 (small effect). Statistically
  detectable with 96,470 orders; the effect size is labelled small, so state on its own separates late from on-time orders only partly.
* Spearman rank correlation with delivery time: freight cost rho = 0.38 (moderate; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.39, n = 96,470); order weight rho = 0.09 (negligible; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.09, n = 96,448).
  Freight and weight are themselves correlated (rho = 0.49), and freight also tracks distance. These do not show that weight or freight *cause* longer delivery.
* **Retrospective, not usable for prediction:** processing time (purchase to carrier hand-over; mean 3.2 days, about 26% of total delivery time).
  Orders in the slowest quarter (4.1+ days) were late 12.1% of the time (n = 24,076) vs 5.0% for the rest
  (n = 72,228); difference +7.1 pp. This is only known after the order was handed to the carrier, and part of the association is plausibly mechanical (a late hand-over leaves less time to arrive).

## 9. Prediction model

**Task.** Predict, from information known at purchase time only, whether an order will arrive after its estimated date
(target: is_late (1 = delivered after the estimated delivery calendar date)). Features: 12 numeric and 4 categorical purchase-time columns
(customer and seller state, product category, same-state flag, order size, price, freight, weight and volume, the checkout delivery promise, day of week).
Outcome-side columns (processing time, review score, status, delivery dates) are excluded; the leakage audit in the metrics file
passed (9 checks).

**Split (chronological, no order appears twice).**

| Partition | Purchase dates | Orders | Late | Late rate |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| train | 2017-01-05 to 2018-03-31 | 64,053 | 5,110 | 7.98% |
| validation | 2018-04-01 to 2018-06-30 | 19,643 | 820 | 4.17% |
| test | 2018-07-01 to 2018-08-29 | 12,507 | 601 | 4.81% |

The late rate differs a lot between partitions (8.0% train, 4.2% validation, 4.8% test), so the
partitions are different regimes. Orders purchased before 2017-01-01 are excluded from modelling (very few orders per month).

**All candidate models** (validation / test; validation figures are tuned and therefore optimistic, test is the untouched later window;
precision / recall / F1 are at each model's own validation-chosen threshold):

| Model | PR-AUC | ROC-AUC | Brier | Log-loss | Precision / recall / F1 (test) | Lift in top 10% (test) |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| Dummy baseline (class prior) | 0.042 / 0.048 | 0.500 / 0.500 | 0.0414 / 0.0468 | 0.1852 / 0.2006 | 0.000 / 0.000 / 0.000 | 1.00x |
| Logistic regression (selected) | 0.140 / 0.073 | 0.781 / 0.617 | 0.0376 / 0.0487 | 0.1508 / 0.2019 | 0.070 / 0.258 / 0.110 | 1.71x |
| Random forest | 0.117 / 0.059 | 0.742 / 0.595 | 0.0383 / 0.0481 | 0.1566 / 0.2042 | 0.054 / 0.251 / 0.088 | 1.19x |
| Histogram gradient boosting | 0.138 / 0.050 | 0.745 / 0.507 | 0.0381 / 0.0504 | 0.1564 / 0.2151 | 0.045 / 0.206 / 0.074 | 1.06x |

PR-AUC of an uninformative model equals the late rate (4.81% on the test window); ROC-AUC of an uninformative model is 0.5. The dummy row is that baseline.

**Selected model: Logistic regression** (isotonic-calibrated), chosen on validation PR-AUC as the simplest model within one bootstrap standard deviation of the best.

* Validation (tuned, optimistic): ROC-AUC 0.781, PR-AUC 0.140, a 3.4x lift over the 4.17% base rate.
* **Test (out of sample, later window): ROC-AUC 0.617 (95% bootstrap interval 0.599 to 0.637),
  PR-AUC 0.073 (interval 0.064 to 0.083) against a no-skill 0.048: a 1.5x lift.**
* At the selected threshold (0.125) the test window gives: 155 late orders caught and 446 missed (recall 25.8%), 2,070 on-time orders flagged
  (precision 7.0%), and 17.8% of all orders flagged. Accuracy (79.9%) is not informative: always predicting "on time" scores 95.2%.
* Probability quality on test: Brier 0.0487 against 0.0468 for always quoting the base rate; log-loss 0.2019 against
  0.2006. The model does NOT beat the constant baseline on Brier score. Mean predicted risk is 7.5% against an observed 4.8%.
* Calibration changed test PR-AUC from 0.079 (uncalibrated) to 0.073.

**Plain assessment.** On the later test window the model's ranking ability is **modest**: ROC-AUC 0.617 (0.5 is chance) and a 1.5x PR-AUC lift
(validation looked much better at 3.4x). Its probabilities are not better calibrated than the base rate, and performance degraded from validation to test.
It should be treated as a coarse screening aid with a modest signal, not as a reliable forecaster, and the stated probabilities should not be read as precise.
Warnings recorded by the training script:

* On the test window the model's Brier score is not better than the constant baseline, so its probabilities are not better calibrated than simply quoting the base rate.
* On the test window the model's log-loss is not better than the constant baseline.
* Test lift (interval 1.3x-1.7x) is clearly below validation lift (3.4x): performance degraded on the later window; expect weaker results in use than the validation figures suggest.
* Calibration lowered test PR-AUC (0.079 uncalibrated -> 0.073).

**Risk bands** (cut points from validation scores; observed late rate by band):

| Band | Validation orders | Validation late rate (95% CI) | Test orders | Test late rate (95% CI) |
| :-- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| Low | 15,571 | 2.2% (1.9% to 2.4%) | 6,890 | 3.1% (2.8% to 3.6%) |
| Moderate | 3,033 | 8.8% (7.8% to 9.8%) | 3,756 | 6.5% (5.8% to 7.4%) |
| High | 1,039 | 21.1% (18.7% to 23.7%) | 1,861 | 7.5% (6.4% to 8.8%) |

On validation the observed late rate rises monotonically from Low to High (2.2% / 8.8% / 21.1%); no adjacent bands overlap. On test the observed late rate rises monotonically from Low to High (3.1% / 6.5% / 7.5%); adjacent bands with overlapping 95% intervals: Moderate-High. The High-to-Low late-rate ratio is 9.8x on validation and 2.4x on test.

**Where the training-to-test mismatch shows up: the same-state relationship reversed.** On the test window the same-state orders were late 7.4% of the time
(n = 5,165) and other-state orders 3.0% (n = 7,342), but the model had mean predicted risk 4.3% for same-state and
9.8% for other-state orders, consistent with the model having learned from the training window, where the pattern ran the other way. In addition 10.1% of test orders
(1,263) have a checkout promise outside the range seen in training (late rate 16.9% for those vs 3.5% for the rest). These are descriptive
observations of drift; they are not shown to be the cause of the weaker test performance, and the data does not show what changed.

**What the model leans on** (permutation importance: drop in PR-AUC when a column is shuffled; predictive association, not cause; the validation column is tuned, the test column is diagnostic):

| Feature (validation rank) | Validation | Test |
| :-- | --: | --: |
| 1. estimated_delivery_days | +0.0703 | +0.0288 |
| 2. customer_state | +0.0579 | +0.0039 |
| 3. same_state | +0.0504 | -0.0194 |
| 4. seller_state | +0.0204 | +0.0107 |
| 5. total_volume_cm3 | +0.0126 | +0.0019 |
| 6. total_freight | +0.0096 | -0.0012 |
| 7. product_category | +0.0083 | +0.0008 |
| 8. max_product_height_cm | +0.0076 | +0.0011 |

Model fitting time recorded in the metrics file: 94 s; trained 2026-10-22 with scikit-learn 1.9.1.

## 10. Data caveats

From `data/processed/data_quality_report.json` (generated 2026-10-22):

* **Only delivered orders are labelled.** 2,963 orders in a non-delivered status (shipped, canceled, unavailable, invoiced, processing, created, approved) and
  8 delivered orders without a delivery date are not in any rate above. Orders still in transit at the end of the data may be disproportionately late, so recent months can be understated. Selection bias / right-censoring: labels exist only for delivered orders. In the test window 145 of 12,824 orders (1.13%) are still in an open status (created/approved/invoiced/processing/shipped) at the end of the data and cannot be labelled; if those orders are disproportionately late, the late rate of the latest months is understated (by at most the share of open orders). Latest recorded delivery: 2018-10-17. Cancelled / unavailable orders are also unlabelled.
* **Timestamp anomalies among delivered orders:** 165 carrier hand-over dates earlier than purchase (processing time set to missing), 23 customer deliveries
  dated before the carrier hand-over, 1,350 hand-overs before payment approval. None affect the late label (which uses purchase, estimate and delivery dates only).
* **Product attributes:** 1,358 analysed orders have no product category (grouped as "unknown"); 4 products have a zero weight and 2 have none
  (22 analysed orders affected). Non-positive weights or dimensions are treated as missing.
* **Multi-item orders:** 9,803 orders have several items, 1,278 several sellers and 727 several categories. Each order is assigned one
  representative seller (largest summed price) and category (highest-priced item), so seller-state, route and category results describe that representative, not the whole basket.
* **Two categories were missing from the official translation file** (pc_gamer, portateis_cozinha_e_preparadores_de_alimentos) and were mapped by a documented supplement.
* **Lateness definition is calendar-date based**: arriving any time on the estimated date counts as on time. The timestamp-based alternative gives 8.11%.
* **One marketplace, 2016-2018, no causal design.** No carrier, weather, holiday, stock or seller-capacity data is available, and customers and sellers cannot be compared on a like-for-like basis.
